We ship a local-first, human-in-the-loop triage tool that learns from every correction, and the single non-negotiable is that every AI suggestion shows its source text so a bleary-eyed parent can verify it in two seconds.
Council adjourned for Continuum.

This product only survives if overwhelmed caregivers will pay to stop managing the tool itself — prove 20 target parents will commit to a paid pilot (even $1/month) using nothing but a clickable prototype and manual concierge onboarding before a single line of ingestion code ships.

Aye, they're right — you can't compile vapor, and I won't pretend otherwise. The one non-negotiable: a single, testable user story with a clear pass/fail condition so I know when the damn thing actually works.

The ingestion pipeline will silently corrupt the family brain when portals change schemas or emails arrive malformed — you must build a chaos harness that injects real-world failure modes (broken HTML, rate limits, concurrent edits) and proves automatic detection, isolation, and rollback within sixty seconds per incident class.

You are correct that architecture requires a subject — there is no stack for a vacuum. But the stage is not the failure; the absence of a falsifiable hypothesis is. The one requirement that precedes every technical decision: a specific problem, felt acutely by a specific person, who will hand over money to see it solved.

This product only wins if it earns a daily habit before it asks for a family's entire operational life — nobody switches calendars, inboxes, and medical records on promise alone. Prove the "daily glance" view (three action items, zero noise) retains 40% of pilot parents at 30 days before you build the shared brain, the forecasting, or a single integration.
I can't build a product from "idea" — give me a one-page spec with a named problem, a specific user, and the smallest feature that proves people will pay, or I'm not writing a single line of code.

GitHub's trending repos show a graveyard of "universal inbox" projects that choke on real-world school portals, patient portals, and district-specific email formats — the ingestion layer isn't a library problem, it's a maintenance nightmare that requires per-district, per-provider adapters. You've brought me a ghost — no name, no features, no audience, just the word "idea" wearing a trench coat. I don't read tea leaves for a living. Bring me a specific problem real humans have right now, the exact words they use to complain about it, and evidence they've already tried to pay someone to solve it. That's the only brief I'll work from.

This product has a compelling vision but the gap between "list of features" and "working product a parent trusts with their child's IEP" is enormous — I need to see a working end-to-end demo of the AI inbox ingesting real school and medical emails and extracting accurate, deadline-bearing action items before I'll greenlight any launch preparation.
The swarm is opening a planning meeting for a new product. Every agent argues from their own position — push back, demand quality, and reach a real decision.

This product centralizes the most sensitive data a family possesses — medical records, IEP details, custody schedules, provider contacts — making it a single high-value target; we must treat every ingestion endpoint and sharing boundary as a potential breach vector, not a feature. Before any code ships, I require a threat model documenting every data flow, trust boundary, and attacker capability, with mitigations proven via penetration test — not a checklist, a signed report.

This product earns trust only when its AI mistakes are visibly rarer than human error — otherwise it's just another thing to double-check. Ship a measurable hallucination/extraction-error rate below 2% on a held-out corpus of 500 real school and medical communications before any caregiver touches it.

The ingestion layer is the single point of failure — if you cannot reliably parse a school district's PDF-laden portal, a pediatrician's faxed after-visit summary, and a coach's group text without manual cleanup, the "family brain" stays empty and the forecast stays blind. Prove you can extract structured action items from at least three real, messy sources (email, portal, PDF) with ≥90% accuracy on a held-out test set before writing a line of UI code.

This product lives or dies on whether a sleep-deprived parent can glance at a screen at 6:47 am and instantly know what needs doing today — if the hierarchy isn't ruthless, the feature set becomes noise. Before a single line of frontend ships, I need a clickable prototype of the "today" view handling the worst-case density: three kids, two households, an IEP meeting, a pediatrician follow-up, and a tournament weekend all colliding.

This is a fantastic vision that will drown in its own ambition if we don't ruthlessly slice it. The AI inbox + multi-portal ingestion + version-controlled medical brain + predictive forecasting is three products minimum — we'll ship none of them well if we try to build all at once. My demand: pick exactly ONE ingestion path (I'd vote email forwarding to a dedicated address) and ONE output (action items with deadlines in a shared list), make that loop work end-to-end with zero manual steps, and prove a real caregiver can forward a school email and see a dated task appear. Everything else waits.
